faq.q: Why is it hot in summer?
faq.a: In summer your half of the Earth tilts towards the Sun. The Sun is high, so its rays hit the ground steeply and concentrate their heat, and the long days give more hours of warming than the short nights can lose.

faq.q: Why is it cold in winter?
faq.a: In winter your half tilts away from the Sun. The low Sun's rays arrive at a slant and spread their heat over a bigger area, and the short days give little time to warm up.

faq.q: Are we closer to the Sun in summer?
faq.a: No. Earth's orbit is nearly a circle, and we are actually closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter. The distance changes by only about 3 percent, which matters far less than the tilt.
asks: Do seasons happen because of distance from the Sun?

faq.q: Why are the seasons opposite in Australia?
faq.a: When the northern half leans towards the Sun, the southern half leans away, and the other way round. So December is summer in Australia and winter in Europe.
asks: Why is Christmas in summer in Australia?

faq.a: Earth's spin axis leans about 23.4 degrees from upright compared with its path round the Sun. Without this tilt there would be almost no seasons.

facts: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees.
Earth is closest to the Sun, about 147 million kilometres away, in early January.
The northern and southern hemispheres always have opposite seasons.
